purpose: Ecallantide is used to treat sudden attacks of hereditary angioedema (HAE) in people aged 12 and older. HAE causes severe swelling that can happen in the face, throat, stomach, hands, feet, or genitals. It is used when an attack is already happening — not to prevent one.
how_it_works: Your body has a protein called plasma kallikrein that, when overactive, triggers swelling attacks in people with HAE. Ecallantide works by blocking this protein so it can't cause the swelling. Think of it like a switch that turns off the signal telling your body to swell up.
common_side_effects: Headache, nausea, diarrhea, fever, stomach pain, and injection site reactions like redness or bruising. Some people may also feel tired or have a runny nose.
warnings: This medication carries a serious risk of a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis, which can happen within an hour after the injection. Because of this risk, it must always be given by a healthcare professional in a medical setting — never at home on your own. Tell your doctor right away if you feel dizzy, have trouble breathing, or notice sudden swelling of the face or throat after receiving the shot.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 30 mg given as three separate injections under the skin (subcutaneous), each injection being 10 mg. If symptoms come back within 24 hours, a second dose of 30 mg may be given. It is always administered by a trained healthcare provider.
